title: IBM Gen AI Engineering cheat sheets

items: 168 hours across 16 courses, self-paced. This bank covers the 10 generative-AI courses (1-3, 10-16), 91 hours.
There is no cumulative exam. Each course has module quizzes you can retake, plus a capstone build project.
Because quizzes are retakeable, passing one proves less than answering an unseen question. That is what this bank is for.
Courses 10-16 build strictly on each other: tokenisation, then embeddings, then attention, then fine-tuning, then alignment, then RAG. Do not skip ahead.
The capstone cannot be simulated. Build it. Everything before it is preparation for that.

head: Trap
Why it catches people
rows: Confusing the AI / ML / DL / gen-AI nesting
Asked constantly in course 1, and the hierarchy is easy to invert under time pressure
Mixing up encoder and decoder roles
BERT and GPT differ by masking, not by 'one uses attention'
Token ids only mean something relative to the vocabulary that produced them
Assuming RAG and fine-tuning are alternatives for the same problem
They solve different problems: facts versus behaviour
Thinking prompt engineering changes the model
It changes nothing; weights are fixed at inference

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Any technique making machines appear intelligent. The outermost set.
Subset of AI that learns patterns from data instead of hand-written rules
Subset of ML using multi-layer neural networks
Subset of deep learning that produces new content
Performs one defined task. Everything in production today.
Human-breadth understanding across arbitrary domains. Does not exist.
Trained broadly at scale, then adapted to many downstream tasks

head: Learning type
Signal it learns from
rows: Labelled examples: input paired with the correct answer
Structure in unlabelled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction)
Rewards and penalties following actions in an environment
Labels derived from the data itself, e.g. predict the masked or next token

head: Generative architecture
How it generates
rows: Generator versus discriminator; the discriminator's judgement trains the generator
Encodes to a distribution over latent space, so sampling it decodes to new data
Learns to reverse a noising process; denoises from pure noise, iteratively
Attention over sequences; the basis of nearly every modern LLM

head: watsonx component
Job
rows: Studio to train, validate, tune and deploy models including foundation models
Lakehouse for storing and querying the data models use
Model risk documentation, drift monitoring, compliance and audit

blocks.text: Accuracy on imbalanced data is a trap: at 97% negatives, a model that always predicts 'negative' scores 97%. Ask for precision, recall or the confusion matrix.

head: Technique
Use when
rows: The task is common and the instruction alone carries it
The format or style is easier to demonstrate than to describe
The answer depends on multiple reasoning steps (arithmetic, logic)
One correct answer exists; sample several chains and take the majority
The model questions you to gather requirements before producing output
Tone, register and vocabulary need shaping. Confers no actual expertise.

items: A good prompt fixes: task, context, audience, format, length and tone. 'Make it good' instructs nothing.
Prefer positive checkable instructions ('at most three sentences') over prohibitions ('do not be verbose').
Delimit user-supplied and retrieved content. It marks the trust boundary as well as the subject.
Temperature scales the sampling distribution: low for extraction and structure, higher for ideation.
Few-shot examples teach everything they share, including properties you did not intend. Vary what should vary.
In long inputs, restate hard constraints near the content they govern; attention to the middle degrades.
Evaluate a prompt change on a fixed set of inputs, not on one output you happened to like.

blocks.text: In-context learning: the model adapts to examples in the prompt without any weight change. It lasts only for that request, which is exactly why RAG works.

head: Tool
What it is for
rows: General linguistic tooling: sentence and word segmentation, stemming, stop words
WordPiece subword tokenisation matching BERT's vocabulary
SentencePiece tokenisation with XLNet's own vocabulary and special tokens
Defines __len__ and __getitem__: how many items and how to fetch item i
Batching, shuffling and parallel loading over a Dataset
Decides how a list of samples becomes one batched tensor — pads variable lengths

items: Always pair a model with its own tokenizer. Other vocabularies produce ids that mean something else.
Subword tokenisation handles unseen words by composing known fragments and keeps the vocabulary small. One token per word is exactly the assumption it abandons.
Pad per batch, not across the dataset; padding to the global maximum wastes compute.
An attention mask tells the model which positions are padding. Omit it and output depends on batch composition.
Load lazily in __getitem__ so memory scales with batch size, not corpus size.
Context window covers prompt and output together, measured in tokens, not words.

head: Representation
Property
rows: Orthogonal: every word equidistant from every other. Length of the vocabulary.
Counts only; word order and syntax discarded
One dense vector per word type. Cannot separate senses of 'bank'.
A different vector per occurrence, computed from surrounding text

head: word2vec variant
Prediction direction
rows: Target word -> context words. More signal per occurrence; better on rare words.
Context words -> target word. Faster to train.

head: Concept
Detail
rows: Next word from the previous N-1. Cannot see beyond the window.
Vanishing/exploding gradients over long sequences; computation is inherently sequential
Gating shortens the gradient path across time. Keeps the sequential bottleneck.
Encoder builds a representation; decoder generates conditioned on it
Feed ground-truth previous token in training. Causes exposure bias at inference.
Each token conditioned on those already produced. N tokens ≈ N forward passes.
Exponentiated average negative log-likelihood. Lower = less surprised by held-out text.
N-gram overlap with references. Punish valid paraphrase; reward copied wording.

head: Component
Purpose
rows: Attention is permutation-invariant; this injects word order
Query·Key gives relevance weights; those weights average the Values
Keeps dot-product variance stable so softmax does not saturate
Parallel heads in different subspaces capture different relationship types
Stops a position attending to later ones, so the decoder cannot read the answer
Decoder queries against encoder keys and values (translation)
Direct gradient path around each sublayer; makes deep stacks trainable
Normalises within one example's features, independent of batch size
Attention moves information between positions; this transforms within one

head: Model
Stack
Pretraining objective
rows: Masked language modelling (~15% masked) + next sentence prediction

head: BERT special token
Role
rows: First position; its output serves as the sequence-level representation
Separates segments and marks the end of a sequence
Marks tokens to be predicted during MLM
Fills to a common batch length; excluded by the attention mask

blocks.text: Self-attention costs scale with the square of sequence length: one score per pair of positions. That single fact drives the whole long-context research agenda.

head: Approach
What it updates
When
rows: Always try first. Instant, free, reversible.
A new head only; backbone frozen
Enough data and compute; strongest adaptation
Small low-rank matrices added to chosen weights
Most of the gain, a fraction of the memory

items: LoRA freezes the base and learns two thin matrices whose product is the weight update. Rank r sets capacity: higher r adapts more and overfits small data sooner.
Because the base is untouched, many adapters share one loaded model at serving time. QLoRA adds 4-bit quantisation of the base.
Fine-tuning learning rates are small (roughly 1e-5 to 5e-5). Rates suited to random initialisation destroy the pretrained representation.
Replace the pretrained head: it predicts the pretraining objective's output space, not your labels.
OOM during training: reduce per-device batch size, then restore the effective batch with gradient accumulation.
Catastrophic forgetting after narrow tuning: mix general data back in, lower the learning rate, train fewer epochs.
Training loss falling while validation loss rises means stop — that is overfitting, not progress.
model.eval() switches dropout off and normalisation to running statistics. torch.no_grad() is separate.

head: Stage
What happens
rows: Train on demonstrations so the model responds sensibly at all
Train a scorer on pairwise human preferences between responses
PPO improves the policy against the reward model, with a KL leash

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The model's conditional distribution over next tokens: state = context, action = token
Scores a response to correlate with human preference. Never generates.
'Which of these two is better' — far less noisy than absolute ratings
Keeps the policy near the frozen reference, preventing reward hacking
Clipped objective stops any single update moving the policy far
High reward-model score, useless output. Hedging and padding are classic symptoms.
Reparameterises the objective so preferences update the policy directly
The intractable normaliser; cancels in DPO's chosen-vs-rejected ratio

blocks.text: PPO needs policy, frozen reference and reward model resident at once. That memory cost is much of why DPO became popular — it needs neither the reward model nor the RL loop.

items: TRL provides SFTTrainer, RewardTrainer, PPOTrainer and DPOTrainer, one per stage.
The reference model is frozen so the KL term has a fixed anchor; if it moved, drift would be unbounded.
Hold out preference data the optimiser never sees, or rising reward is indistinguishable from memorisation.
Climb the ladder in order: prompt, then SFT on demonstrations, then preference methods only when you can judge better-versus-worse but cannot write the right answer.

head: Stage
Happens when
rows: Offline. Loaders normalise PDF/HTML/CSV into Documents with metadata.
Offline. Size and overlap decide whether a passage holds a whole answer.
Offline. Vectors live in the embedding model's space.
Per request, with the same embedding model
Per request. Trades recall against noise and prompt cost.
Per request, conditioned on the retrieved passages

head: LangChain component
Role
rows: Reads a source format into Documents with metadata
Chunks documents; chunk_size and chunk_overlap are the levers
Chooses which few-shot examples to include for this input
Turns model text into structured data; supplies format instructions
Interface: query in, documents out. Backend can be anything.
Composition where each step's output feeds the next
Chooses actions via tools, observes results, decides what to do next

head: Retrieval concept
Detail
rows: Separate question and context encoders, aligned so questions land near answering passages
Efficient nearest-neighbour search over dense vectors. Stores and searches only.
Too few: answer absent. Too many: signal diluted, prompt cost up.
Ensures content across a boundary appears whole in at least one chunk

blocks.text: Changing the embedding model invalidates the whole index — old and new vectors live in incomparable spaces. The corpus must be re-embedded. Generators swap freely; embedders do not.

items: Topically right chunks that never contain the answer = a chunking problem, not a model problem.
Good retrieval with poor answers = a generation problem: context assembly, instructions or generator choice.
Similarity search always returns its nearest neighbours however far away. Out-of-scope questions need a relevance threshold or a grading step.
Instruct the model to answer only from context and to say when the context does not contain the answer.
Deleting a source document does nothing until its chunks are removed from the index.
Treat retrieved and user-supplied text as data, never as instructions. Fence it and keep it out of the privileged section.
RAG over fine-tuning when facts change or answers must cite sources; fine-tuning for stable behaviour and style.
